A1.justification: Both PDFs describe KineMask. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite the changed title and layout.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments, qualitative real-world generations, ablations and a 30-participant user study.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, a backbone ablation and edited-scene experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the stated second-stage dropout rule from retaining a prefix through a cutoff frame to retaining sampled frame indices. The architecture, losses and inference remain unchanged. Figure 2 still describes dropping final frames, leaving implementation details inconsistent.

E1.justification: Simple Motion, Interactions and Real World remain the datasets. Figure 7 adds an environmental-intervention scenario: at fixed input velocity, the collision partner is removed or replaced with different objects. This extends tested scene conditions without adding a benchmark.

E2.justification: TORA and MotionI2V join the user study and qualitative comparisons; PhysGen3D receives a new qualitative comparison. The effects-of-data table drops Wan and Force Prompting, although Wan's unchanged scores reappear in the backbone comparison. This substantially broadens comparison methods while reducing one existing comparison.

E3.justification: Added evaluations introduce Wan-backbone training, trajectory endpoints for TORA/MotionI2V, and fixed-velocity scene-edit controls. Existing dataset splits, training budget, metrics and participant count remain. Revised IoU wording does not establish whether ground-truth mask preprocessing actually changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds a quantitative and qualitative backbone ablation (Table 4, Figure 12) and object-removal/replacement tests of collision behavior (Figure 7). It also expands difficult-object comparisons and failure examples. These substantially extend analyses of portability and scene-dependent behavior; existing training, caption, encoding and sampling ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report single metric values and user-preference percentages without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The additional results follow the same reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figure 4 adds motion/interactions/physical preferences of 51/68/59% against TORA and 86/86/77% against MotionI2V. Table 4 adds KineMask-Wan results, including FVD 475.6 and IoU 0.257. New qualitative outcomes and removal of Force Prompting's quantitative row further change the evidence. Retained core scores are unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 6 replaces the scalar cutoff condition f <= f* with membership f in f*, redefining the mask selection mathematically. Other diffusion and training equations remain substantively unchanged; neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: Both retain the central contributions: two-stage velocity-mask conditioning, synthetic-to-real interaction generalization, and complementary text conditioning with advantages over comparable-size models. The revised rigid-body wording makes an already established scope more explicit rather than introducing a different core claim.

C2.justification: v2 interprets edited-object outcomes as mass awareness and contrasts inferred endpoints with trajectory control. It adds explanations for selecting CogVideoX over Wan, discusses PhysGen3D reconstruction failures, and identifies soft-body interactions as future work. Existing failure-mode explanations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents trajectory endpoints and mask inputs for added baselines and clarifies automatic arrow-to-mask conversion. Training hyperparameters and prompts remain. v1's reproducibility statement and explicit code/model/data release pledge disappear, although the project link remains; this does not establish actual resource withdrawal.

R1.justification: Related work expands to include PhysGen3D, Motion-I2V, iPOKE and additional trajectory-control research. Positioning more explicitly distinguishes initial-velocity conditioning from predefined trajectories and dataset-specific training, while retaining the original research direction.

P1.justification: The title changes, terminology emphasizes rigid bodies and object-level control, and several introductory and analytical paragraphs are tightened. Acknowledgements and the reproducibility statement are removed. The main section sequence and much of the explanatory prose remain.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout, moves the teaser to the first page, and separates former Figure 5b into Table 1. Figures are resized and reorganized, with expanded user-study, causality, comparison and failure panels throughout the appendices.

improvement.justification: The added trajectory-based and simulation-based comparisons, backbone ablation and scene interventions provide useful validation beyond v1's narrower evidence. Gains are limited by unchanged core quantitative results, qualitative support for the mass-awareness interpretation, and inconsistent dropout descriptions. The removed release pledge also reduces reproducibility information, but the broader empirical assessment provides a modest net improvement.
